summary: Psalm 68 begins by calling on God to rise against enemies and to make the righteous rejoice. It remembers God leading his people through the wilderness, providing for the poor, scattering kings, and entering the sanctuary in triumph. The psalm ends by summoning all kingdoms to sing to God, whose strength is over Israel and whose power strengthens his people.
whyItMatters: This chapter gathers many major psalm themes into one crowded praise poem: rescue, procession, sanctuary, judgment, care for the vulnerable, and the nations called to acknowledge God. It stands within Book II of Psalms, where David-associated prayers and wider royal hope are prominent.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David,” but Psalms as a book is an anthology, and Davidic headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities receiving the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The Psalms were composed and collected over time; the exact date of Psalm 68 is uncertain.
context.setting: The poem moves through images of wilderness, Sinai, battle, mountains, sanctuary, Jerusalem, and the kingdoms of the earth rather than narrating one simple setting.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and praise, with sharp images, changes of address, communal summons, and the performance marker “Selah.”

outline.heading: God Rises and the Righteous Rejoice
outline.note: The psalm opens with God scattering enemies, while the righteous rejoice and God is named as protector of the fatherless, widows, lonely, and prisoners.

outline.heading: God Marches from the Wilderness
outline.note: The poem remembers God going before the people, the earth trembling at Sinai, and God providing rain and goodness for the weary and poor.

outline.heading: Kings Flee and Plunder Is Shared
outline.note: A proclaimed word leads to fleeing armies, divided plunder, and the scattered kings described with vivid poetic images.

outline.heading: God Chooses His Mountain
outline.note: The rugged mountains of Bashan are contrasted with the mountain where God chooses to reign, and God is pictured with countless chariots ascending in triumph.

outline.heading: Deliverance and Judgment
outline.note: The psalm blesses God as the one who bears burdens and gives escape from death, then turns to severe images of judgment against enemies.

outline.heading: Procession into the Sanctuary
outline.note: The people see God's procession into the sanctuary, tribes and musicians are named, and the prayer asks God to strengthen his work and restrain warlike nations.

outline.heading: All Kingdoms Called to Praise
outline.note: The closing summons the kingdoms of the earth to sing to God, ascribing strength to the God of Israel who gives strength and power to his people.

keyVerses.text: A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the psalm's claim that God's power is not only military or cosmic but also protective toward vulnerable people.

keyVerses.text: You have ascended on high. You have led away captives. You have received gifts among people, yes, among the rebellious also, that Yah God might dwell there.
keyVerses.why: This verse stands at the poem's triumphal center, joining ascent, captives, gifts, rebellion, and God's dwelling.

keyVerses.text: Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears our burdens, even the God who is our salvation. Selah.
keyVerses.why: After the large public images, this verse states the chapter's trust in direct and personal terms.

keyVerses.text: You are awesome, God, in your sanctuaries. The God of Israel gives strength and power to his people. Praise be to God!
keyVerses.why: The final verse gathers sanctuary, awe, Israel, strength, and praise into the psalm's closing confession.

questions.question: What kind of writing is Psalm 68?
questions.answer: It is a praise psalm with many compressed poetic movements rather than a straightforward story. It moves from battle language to care for vulnerable people, from wilderness memory to sanctuary procession, and from Israel to the kingdoms of the earth.

questions.question: Does the heading prove David wrote every word of the psalm?
questions.answer: The chapter's heading says, “A Psalm by David,” so the received text associates it with David. Psalm headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging, and readers differ on how much each heading establishes historically.

questions.question: Who are the “fatherless” and “widows”?
questions.answer: They are named as people for whom God acts as father and defender. The verse does not present them as symbols only; it uses them to show that God's rule includes protection for those without ordinary social protection.

questions.question: What is “Selah”?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears in this chapter after verses 7, 19, and 32. It is an uncertain musical or performance marker, so it is safest to notice it as a signal of voiced worship without claiming exactly what ancient performers did there.

questions.question: Why does the psalm talk about Sinai?
questions.answer: Verses 7-10 recall God going before the people, marching through the wilderness, and appearing as “the God of Sinai.” The point inside this chapter is memory: the God praised in the sanctuary is the same God remembered as leading, shaking the earth, sending rain, and providing for the poor.

questions.question: What is happening with Bashan, the mountain, and the sanctuary?
questions.answer: Verses 15-18 contrast the majestic mountains of Bashan with the mountain where God chooses to reign. The psalm does not pause to explain the geography; poetically, the chosen dwelling of God matters more than impressive height or ruggedness.

questions.question: Why are verses 21-23 so violent?
questions.answer: These verses picture God striking enemies and bringing them back for judgment in severe battle imagery. Readers should not turn the description into personal permission for revenge; within the psalm, the violence belongs to God's defeat of enemies and is placed beside claims that God delivers and saves.

questions.question: Why are Egypt and Ethiopia mentioned near the end?
questions.answer: The psalm's horizon widens beyond Israel. It says princes will come from Egypt, Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God, and then it calls “kingdoms of the earth” to sing to God.

questions.question: How should a first-time reader follow such a crowded psalm?
questions.answer: Track the repeated movement of God: God arises, goes before the people, enters the sanctuary, commands strength, and is praised by the kingdoms. The details are dense, but the main motion is from God's victory and care to public worship and worldwide summons.

glossary.def: A shortened divine name used in verse 4: “to Yah, his name!”
People without a father named in verse 5 as receiving God's fatherly care.
Women whose husbands have died; verse 5 names them as people for whom God is a defender.
A preserved performance marker in verses 7, 19, and 32 whose exact ancient function is uncertain.
A place named in verses 15 and 22, associated here with rugged mountains and with God's power to bring people back.
The holy place into which God's procession is seen in verse 24, and where God is praised in verse 35.
